sentences.text: A city of 83,000. In three days, 72,000 people arrived.
How did they get in? Why that week? Could it happen again?
This is Ceuta: Spain, but in Africa.
Its border with Morocco is a double fence, and it stops at the sea.
So in late July, tens of thousands swam around it.
But here's the weird part: they thought the border was open.
Three problems collided.
Geography: Europe is one short swim away.
Politics: in June, Spain's top court ruled that swimmers can't be sent straight back.
Social: next door in Fnideq, young people have few jobs since the border trade closed.
Now it gets strange: on Facebook, that ruling became a rumour: the border is open.
All three met in one week.
Within days, almost all went back.
But at least 80 people died.
And Italy brought back border checks on travellers from Spain.
Then a new rumour named a date: 15 August.
Morocco sent thousands of police and soldiers, and stopped it.
It's not the first time: in May 2021, thousands crossed too.
So, could it happen again? This big, not soon.
Smaller swims? Almost surely: the jobs and the sea haven't changed.
And the dotted line at the start? A floating barrier, to make sending swimmers back legal again.
Save this for the next border crisis.
Should Spain send swimmers back at once?
